info.title: blip API
info.summary: Read uptime, latency and incident data for your monitors.
info.description:
The blip API is read-only and returns JSON. It serves the same monitor data as the status page: current status, daily and hourly uptime, every raw check, and incidents with their notes.

Every endpoint works without credentials for **public** monitors. An API key adds private monitors and each monitor's method and URL.

```sh
curl "$BLIP_URL/api/monitors" -H "Authorization: Bearer $BLIP_KEY"
```

## Authentication

Create a key in the panel under **API**, then send it as a bearer token in the `Authorization` header.

Keys look like `blip_k7m2q9xd_3f8hw2c9tqzv6n1mbxr4e5ka`. The first part, `blip_k7m2q9xd`, is the key's public prefix, which the panel lists so you can tell keys apart. The rest is the secret. blip stores only a hash of it and shows it once, when the key is created or rotated.

- A key sees exactly the monitors it was scoped to (or all of them), public or private.
- An invalid, revoked, rotated or expired key gets `401`. It never falls back to public data, so a broken integration fails loudly.
- Keys are read-only. They can't change monitors or reach the panel's own endpoints.
- Rotating a key issues a new secret and restarts its expiry. The old secret stops working at once.

Requests without an `Authorization` header see public monitors only, without their method and URL. Signed-in panel sessions see everything.

## Errors

Errors use standard HTTP status codes with a JSON body holding one message:

```json
{ "error": "API key has expired" }
```

- `401`: the key is malformed, unknown or expired. The response carries `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`.
- `404`: the monitor doesn't exist **or** the caller can't see it. The two are indistinguishable on purpose.
- `500`: an unexpected server error. Retry with backoff.

## Time and units

- Timestamps are Unix seconds, UTC.
- `ms` is latency in milliseconds.
- `code` is the HTTP status a check received, or a negative value when no response arrived: `0` connection error, `-1` timeout, `-2` DNS failure, `-3` connection refused, `-4` TLS error, `-5` the response arrived but its health body reported failure. Statuses 200–399 count as up.
- Hourly buckets align to UTC hours. Daily buckets start at local midnight for the `tz` offset you pass.
- Buckets are sparse: hours and days without checks are left out.
- Ranges are half-open: `from` is included, `to` is not.

## Health bodies

When a check's response body describes the service's health, blip reads it. It recognises the IETF `application/health+json` draft, Spring Boot Actuator, MicroProfile Health, ASP.NET Core HealthChecks, Atlassian Statuspage, Elasticsearch cluster health, one-word bodies such as `Healthy` or `Degraded`, and plain JSON with familiar field names such as `status`, `version`, `commit`, `uptime`, `started_at` and `hostname`. A monitor can also point at its own fields, or turn this off.

- A body reporting **fail** marks the check down with code `-5`, even with a `200` status, and opens an incident naming the failing components.
- **warn** keeps the check up but marks it degraded: `Check.health` is `warn` and buckets count it in `warn`.
- **maintenance** keeps the check up.
- The latest body is summarised in `Monitor.report`. Callers without a key or session get only its status.
- When a check's body can't be read (a proxy's error page, say), `report` keeps the last one that could. Compare `report.t` with `last.t` to tell.
- Changing a monitor's method, URL or health settings hides its earlier report and starts tracking afresh, so pointing at a different version field isn't logged as a deploy.
- Version changes and process restarts become events. A new version must be seen on two checks in a row, so a rollout flapping between old and new instances logs one deploy. Start times come from a `started_at`-style field or from `uptime`, whose unit blip learns from how fast it grows. A process first seen behind a load balancer only counts as restarted if it started after the previous check.

## Retention

Raw checks are kept for 30 days, and hourly rollups and events for 400 days, by default. An admin can change both in the panel, so older ranges may come back shorter than requested.

tags.name: Monitors
tags.description: Monitors and their history. Every response is filtered to what the caller may see.

tags.name: Meta
tags.description: This document and the service's health.

get.description: Returns every monitor the caller can see, sorted by name, each with its latest check and recent daily uptime.

parameters.name: days
parameters.description: How many days of daily buckets to include, counting today.

200.description: The visible monitors. An empty array when there are none.

get.description: Returns one monitor with its latest check and up to 400 days of daily uptime.

parameters.name: days
parameters.description: How many days of daily buckets to include, counting today.

get.description: Returns hourly rollups for a time range, oldest first. Rollups outlive raw checks, so this is the way to read history older than the raw retention window. A span longer than 31 days is shortened by moving `from` forward.

200.description: Hourly buckets whose start falls in the range.

get.description: Returns every check in a time range, oldest first, up to 20,000 of them. A span longer than 7 days is shortened by moving `from` forward. To page through a busy monitor, repeat the request with `from` set to one second after the last check's `t`.
Returns a monitor's most recent incidents, newest first, with their notes. An incident opens at the first failed check and closes at the next successful one.
Returns version changes and process restarts read from the monitor's health bodies, newest first. Callers without a key or session get only each event's `t` and `kind`.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start of the range, Unix seconds (inclusive). Defaults to 90 days before `to`.

get.description: Returns this document as OpenAPI 3.1 JSON. Import it into Postman, Insomnia or a client generator. It is served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` so browser-based tools can load it.
Answers `ok` while the server is running. Suited to load balancers and container health checks.

apiKey.description: An API key created in the panel under **API**, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.

id.name: id
id.description: The monitor's ID, as returned by `listMonitors`.

tz.name: tz
tz.description: Your UTC offset in seconds east of UTC, so daily buckets start at your local midnight. For example `19800` for UTC+05:30 or `-18000` for UTC−05:00.

from.name: from
from.description: Start of the range, Unix seconds (inclusive). Defaults to one day before `to`.

to.name: to
to.description: End of the range, Unix seconds (exclusive). Defaults to now.

Unauthorized.description: The `Authorization` header holds a malformed, unknown, revoked or expired key.

NotFound.description: No such monitor, or the caller can't see it.

Monitor.description: An HTTP endpoint that blip checks on a fixed interval.

id.description: Stable ID. IDs of deleted monitors are never reused.

method.description: HTTP method used for checks. Only present for API keys and signed-in users.

url.description: The URL being checked. Only present for API keys and signed-in users.

public.description: Whether the monitor is listed on the public status page.

last.description: The most recent check, or `null` before the first one.

report.description: What the latest health body said, or `null` if no body has been understood yet.

days.description: Daily buckets, oldest first, starting at local midnight for the requested `tz`. Days without checks are left out.

t.description: When the check ran, Unix seconds.

code.description: HTTP status, or `0` connection error, `-1` timeout, `-2` DNS failure, `-3` connection refused, `-4` TLS error, `-5` health body reported failure. 200–399 is up.

health.description: The status the response body reported. Left out when the body said nothing blip understood.

Bucket.description: Checks aggregated over an hour or a day.

t.description: Start of the bucket, Unix seconds.

up.description: How many of them were up. Uptime is `up / n`.

warn.description: How many of the up checks reported degraded health.

ms.description: Mean response time of the successful checks, or `0` if none succeeded.

HealthConfig.description: How a monitor's response bodies are read. Only present for API keys and signed-in users. Each path overrides detection for one field, as a dotted path into the JSON body such as `app.build.version` or `checks.0.status`.

started.description: Path to the process start time: an ISO 8601 date or a Unix time in seconds or milliseconds.

uptime.description: Path to the uptime: a number, whose unit blip learns, or a duration such as `72h3m` or `PT3H`.

instance.description: Path to an ID naming the instance that answered.

Report.description: The latest health body, as blip understood it. Callers without a key or session get only `t` and `status`.

t.description: When the body was read, Unix seconds.

status.description: The overall status. Empty when the body gave other details but no status.

version.description: The release, with the short commit when both are given.

started.description: When the process started, Unix seconds.

message.description: The body's own message, if any.

components.description: Dependencies the body reported on, such as databases and caches.

Component.description: One dependency in a health body.

output.description: What the component said about itself.

Event.description: A change noticed between health bodies.

t.description: When it happened, Unix seconds: when the new version was first seen, or when the process started.

kind.description: `deploy`: the version changed. `restart`: a known process started again. `start`: a new instance appeared.

instance.description: The instance, when the body names one.

start.description: Time of the first failed check, Unix seconds.

ended.description: Time of the first successful check after it, or `null` while ongoing.

notes.description: Notes added by the team, oldest first.

author.description: The author's email for signed-in users. Empty for API keys and anonymous callers, since keys are often given to third parties.

t.description: When the note was added, Unix seconds.
